passage:
Day one: Pradeep, five, puffed out his cheeks at the dinner table in their Jaipur flat after being told to finish his dal. His father Chaitanya laughed. "You look like a fish!" Pradeep giggled and blew out.
Day four: Pradeep puffed his cheeks again, but this time his brows were low and his arms crossed after losing at ludo. Chaitanya sat down. "This one looks different. Are you really cross?"
"Yes," muttered Pradeep, letting the air out slowly.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do with his cheeks at the dinner table on day one?
qa.a: He puffed out his cheeks.

qa.q: What made Chaitanya think the second puff was different from the first, and what does it show about Pradeep's feeling?
qa.a: This time Pradeep's brows were low and his arms crossed, so Chaitanya guessed he was really cross after losing. The first puff looked more like a joke.

qa.q: What would you advise Chaitanya to do the next time Pradeep puffs his cheeks?
qa.a: He can check the tone and body, as he did, and ask gently which kind it is before he laughs or scolds.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when his father asks "Are you really cross?"
qa.a: He may feel understood and less alone with the feeling, which may be why he answered honestly and let the air out slowly.

grounding: A cheek puff can be playful or real irritation, and tone and body show which.

passage: On a wet Sunday, Aadhya sat on the sofa with her cheeks puffed and her chin high, watching her mother Ira pack the umbrella away. The park trip had been cancelled. The puff looked like theatre: Aadhya glanced sideways to see if Ira noticed, and one corner of her mouth twitched. "Very dramatic!" said Ira. Aadhya let out a giggle, then puffed again and let her voice wobble. "But it's raining, Amma." Ira sat beside her. "I'm sad about it too. Shall we build a fort?"

qa.q: Why was the park trip cancelled?
qa.a: It was raining.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's sideways glance suggest about her puffed cheeks, and what else might they mean?
qa.a: The glance and the twitching mouth suggest she was partly acting for her mother's reaction. Her wobbling voice later hints that some disappointment was real too.

qa.q: What could Ira do to help with the disappointment?
qa.a: She could name her own sadness about the trip and offer a fun alternative, such as building a fort.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Aadhya puffs her cheeks at her?
qa.a: She may feel amused at first, then a little sorry for the real disappointment beneath the theatre.

grounding: A cheek puff can be partly theatre and partly real feeling, and the child's glance and voice show the mix.

passage: “Bath time, Chinmay,” Ramesh called across the flat. Chinmay stood in the doorway, folded his arms and puffed out his cheeks like a balloon. Ramesh looked closer. Chinmay's eyes were twinkling, and one cheek was already leaking air in a giggle. “Oh no,” said Ramesh, “a grumpy frog in my house.” Chinmay burst out laughing and hopped toward the bathroom. Ramesh smiled. On Monday the same puffed cheeks had come with stamping and tears, and that time he had sat with Chinmay instead.

qa.q: What did Ramesh call Chinmay?
qa.a: A grumpy frog.

qa.q: How can you tell that Chinmay was feeling playful, not cross, this time?
qa.a: His eyes were twinkling and he was starting to giggle, which suggests he was feeling playful. On another day the same face came with stamping and tears, which showed real upset.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Ramesh read the twinkling eyes and played along with the frog joke, which turned bath time into a game instead of a fight. 😊

qa.q: Why might Ramesh react differently on a day like Monday?
qa.a: On Monday the puffed cheeks came with stamping and tears, so he treated it as real upset and sat with Chinmay instead of joking.

grounding: A preschooler puffs his cheeks as comic theatre, and his father reads the playful tone and body before responding.

passage:
“Zubin, dinner!” Vikas called.
Zubin puffed out his cheeks and turned away.
“Is that a funny face or a cross face?” Vikas asked.
“Cross!” Zubin's voice cracked. He kicked the carpet. “Mishti knocked my tower down.”
“Ah. That's a real cross face, then.” Vikas sat on the floor. “The tall one with the flag?”
Zubin nodded, cheeks still puffed, fists tight.
“That's annoying. Shall we build it again after dinner?”
Zubin let out his breath. “Only if Mishti doesn't touch it.”

qa.q: Who knocked Zubin's tower down?
qa.a: Mishti.

qa.q: How did Zubin's voice and body show what his puffed cheeks meant?
qa.a: His voice cracked, he kicked the carpet and his fists were tight, which shows he was truly angry and frustrated, not playing. He may also have been sad about losing the tall tower.

qa.q: What could Vikas try at dinner to help?
qa.a: He could keep the promise to rebuild the tower after dinner and talk with Zubin about a safe place for it so Mishti doesn't touch it.

qa.q: How might Mishti see Zubin's puffed cheeks?
qa.a: Mishti might think it is a silly game face, not realising Zubin is really upset about the tower.

grounding: A child's puffed cheeks carry real irritation, and his father checks tone and body before deciding what it means.

passage:
Note by Omkar, dance teacher, Saturday class.
Mohit puffs his cheeks at clean-up time most weeks. Usually he does it with a wiggle and a side-look at his friends, and they all laugh; I laugh too and hand him the scarves. Today it was different. He puffed his cheeks, but his shoulders were up and he wouldn't move. I asked quietly, “Real cross or funny cross?” He whispered, “Real. I didn't get a turn.” I gave him the first turn next week, and he helped fold scarves.

qa.q: What did Mohit whisper when Omkar asked him?
qa.a: “Real. I didn't get a turn.”

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling at clean-up this Saturday?
qa.a: He felt left out and frustrated because he did not get a turn, and the puffed cheeks were real irritation. On other weeks the same face was playful, a joke to make his friends laugh.

qa.q: How did Omkar tell the difference between the two kinds of puffed cheeks?
qa.a: Omkar looked at Mohit's body: a wiggle and a side-look meant a joke, while raised shoulders and refusing to move meant real upset, and then asked quietly.

qa.q: How might Mohit's friends see his puffed cheeks today?
qa.a: They might expect the usual joke and laugh, not noticing he was really upset this time.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler's cheek puff being sometimes theatre and sometimes real irritation, with body cues showing which.

passage:
On the verandah of their small-town house, Trisha cut the last mango and said, "That's all for today."

Mahima puffed out her cheeks like two balloons, crossed her eyes and let out a loud "Hmph!" Then she peeked at her cousin and giggled. Trisha puffed her cheeks back, and they both laughed.

That evening, when Trisha switched off the cartoons, Mahima puffed her cheeks again. This time she turned her back, arms folded, and stamped into the other room without a sound.

qa.q: What did Trisha cut on the verandah?
qa.a: The last mango.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling the second time she puffed her cheeks?
qa.a: She was probably truly irritated about the cartoons being switched off; turning her back, folding her arms and stamping away show real annoyance. She may also have been tired by evening.

qa.q: How could Trisha tell the two cheek puffs apart?
qa.a: By watching the rest of Mahima: giggling and peeking meant theatre, while a turned back, folded arms and silence meant real crossness.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha treated both puffs as a joke?
qa.a: She might tease Mahima when she was really upset, and Mahima could feel laughed at instead of understood.

grounding: It shows the same cheek puff as comic theatre in one moment and real irritation in another, with the body showing which.
